title: What is EBS, what are the volume types (gp3/gp2 general-purpose SSD, io1/io2 provisioned IOPS, st1/sc1 HDD), and why is gp3 usually preferred over gp2 (decoupled IOPS/throughput, cheaper)?
shortTitle: EBS, Volume Types, and Why gp3 Over gp2
keyPoints: EBS is persistent, network-attached block storage for EC2 that survives instance stops and terminations.
gp3 is the preferred general-purpose SSD because it decouples IOPS and throughput from volume size and costs roughly twenty percent less than gp2.
gp2 ties performance to size at three IOPS per GiB, so small volumes are slow and you must over-provision capacity just to get speed.
io1 and io2 provisioned-IOPS SSDs deliver the highest consistent performance for latency-critical databases like the core banking ledger.
st1 and sc1 are HDD types optimized for large sequential throughput at low cost and cannot be used as boot volumes.
Migrating from gp2 to gp3 is done live with Elastic Volumes, with no downtime required.
gp3 provides a baseline of 3000 IOPS and 125 MB/s regardless of size, tunable up to 16000 IOPS and 1000 MB/s.

s1_definition.oneliner: EBS is a persistent virtual disk for EC2, and gp3 beats gp2 because you tune IOPS and throughput separately from size and pay less.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **EBS (Elastic Block Store)** – a durable, network-attached block storage service for EC2 instances that behaves like a virtual hard disk and persists independently of the instance lifecycle.
- **gp2 and gp3** – general-purpose SSD volume types suitable for most workloads such as boot volumes and medium databases.
- **io1 and io2** – provisioned-IOPS SSD types for the highest, most consistent low-latency performance, used for critical transactional databases.
- **st1 (throughput-optimized) and sc1 (cold)** – HDD types designed for large, sequential workloads at low cost; they cannot serve as boot volumes.
- **gp3 advantage** – decouples IOPS and throughput from volume size and is roughly twenty percent cheaper per GiB than gp2.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an EC2 server as a desk where a clerk at National Bank of India works, and EBS as the filing cabinet bolted next to the desk. The cabinet holds all the clerk's documents, and even if the clerk goes home (the instance stops), the cabinet and its documents stay. gp2 is an older cabinet where the speed of pulling out files depends on how big the cabinet is – a small cabinet is slow. gp3 is a newer cabinet where you can dial the speed up or down separately from the size, and it costs less, so you pay only for the speed you actually need.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Amazon Elastic Block Store, or EBS, is durable network-attached block storage for EC2 instances. It behaves like a virtual hard disk that the operating system formats and uses like a local drive, but it is replicated within an Availability Zone for durability and persists independently of the instance. If I stop or terminate the instance, the volume and its data survive and can be re-attached elsewhere.

There are four families of volume types. The general-purpose SSDs, gp2 and gp3, cover most workloads like boot volumes and medium databases. The provisioned-IOPS SSDs, io1 and io2, deliver the highest and most consistent performance for latency-critical workloads like the core banking ledger. The HDDs, st1 and sc1, are magnetic and tuned for large sequential throughput at low cost, suited to log processing and cold data, and they cannot be boot volumes.

The reason gp3 is almost always preferred over gp2 is that gp2 ties performance to size at three IOPS per gigabyte, so a small volume is slow and you end up over-provisioning capacity just to buy speed. gp3 decouples performance from size entirely: it gives a flat 3000 IOPS and 125 MB/s baseline regardless of volume size, and I can raise IOPS and throughput independently up to 16000 IOPS and 1000 MB/s. On top of this, gp3 is roughly twenty percent cheaper per gigabyte, and I can migrate from gp2 to gp3 live using Elastic Volumes with no downtime.

At National Bank of India, the reporting service ran a 100 GiB gp2 data volume that gave only 300 baseline IOPS, and the team wanted to inflate it to a terabyte just to get speed. I moved it to gp3, which gave a 3000 IOPS baseline on the same 100 GiB and let me provision up to 6000 IOPS without buying unused space, cutting cost at the same time. The one place I kept provisioned-IOPS io2 was the core ledger database, because it needs more than 16000 IOPS and demands rock-solid consistent low latency.

Remember one sentence: gp3 decouples IOPS and throughput from volume size, gives a 3000 IOPS baseline regardless of capacity, and costs about twenty percent less than gp2, making it the default EBS choice for almost every workload.
